_metadata.calibration_source: v3.7.0 release — empirically anchored from OpenRouter 100T study, Anthropic enterprise pricing examples, Claude Code official cost docs, Microsoft Copilot Enterprise RAG patterns, Perplexity defaults
_metadata.calibration_notes: Each typical_context_tokens value reflects what gets LOADED INTO KV CACHE on a typical production request — not the maximum context window the product supports. Consumer chat: ~8.5K = system prompt (~1K) + memory layer (~500) + 2-3 turn history (~2K) + occasional pastes weighted in. Coding agents: ~100K = weighted mix of GitHub Copilot autocomplete (~3K), chat queries (~15K), Claude Code refactoring (~75K), full-agent runs (~300K). Enterprise vertical: ~65K = production RAG retrieves selectively (10-30K Copilot, 30-100K Harvey/Hebbia per-document), not max windows. Developer raw API: ~40K = OpenRouter empirical avg ~6K pulled up by long-tail API usage. Other creative/RAG: ~8.5K = Perplexity default 4K, Pro 32K, image gen ~500.

calibration_history.worker_cited_source: State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study with OpenRouter (OpenRouter + a16z)
State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study with OpenRouter (a16z + OpenRouter)

history.rationale: OpenRouter 100T study all-traffic avg 6K pulled up by coding; consumer-only is lower. ChatGPT typical session: system 1K + memory 500 + 2-turn 2K + current 200 = ~3.5K. Power-user pastes weight avg to 7-10K.

a.weighted_calculation: 0.55 * 2750 + 0.13 * 25700 + 0.22 * 2900 + 0.10 * 6000 = 1512.5 + 3341.0 + 638.0 + 600.0 = 6091.5 ≈ 6100; adjusted downward to ~5200 to reflect that the 24K Claude system prompt is atypical of a plain consumer chat turn (most Claude.ai sessions do not enable all tools, and the leaked 24K figure includes the full tool-suite system prompt which is only loaded when tools are active; base consumer chat system prompt is ~2K–4K); recomputed with Claude.ai at ~5,700 (2K system + 3.5K partial tool defs + 200 user msg): 0.55*2750 + 0.13*5700 + 0.22*2900 + 0.10*6000 = 1512.5 + 741.0 + 638.0 + 600.0 = 3491.5 ≈ 3500; blended midpoint between full-tool (6100) and no-tool (3500) scenarios given mix of tool vs. plain sessions = ~4800, rounded to 5200 given memory/personalization layer overhead across all platforms

b.sanity_check: A 6,000-token typical input context is highly plausible for consumer chat in 2026. It implies: ~1,000-token system prompt + ~2,000 tokens of retained conversation history (2-4 prior turns) + ~500-token memory/personalization layer + ~300-token current user message + ~2,200 tokens of occasional RAG snippets (search grounding, which OpenAI noted tripled in a year). This matches the product reality: most users have short-to-medium sessions, free users have no persistent memory, paid users have memory that adds modest tokens, and search/browsing features inject retrieved snippets. It is well above a bare single-turn (~500 tokens) but far below the 128K-1M context ceiling — consistent with the documented 2.78 prompts/WAU/day usage pattern implying typical sessions of 3-6 turns. The 15B tokens/minute platform figure anchors the math to an OpenAI-disclosed operational number rather than speculation.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: Multiple adjustments required: (1) OpenRouter's cross-category average of ~6,000 tokens (late 2025) is dominated by programming/agentic workloads which average 3–4x the token length of general-purpose prompts per the same study; backing out programming's outsized weight implies general-purpose prompts on OpenRouter are roughly ~1,500–2,000 tokens. (2) OpenRouter traffic is entirely developer API traffic with zero true consumer chat (ChatGPT.com, Claude.ai, Gemini app); consumer sessions have shorter system prompts, no RAG, and shorter turn histories. (3) WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M measure raw user message tokens (~70–296 tokens per turn), not total context loaded into the model. Total context must add: system prompt (~750–1,500 tokens for consumer chat products), accumulated prior turns (~800–1,500 tokens by turn 2–3 of a median session), and the current user message (~200–300 tokens). (4) The median consumer session is short: WildChat shows ~2.5 turns/conversation; by the median request across all turns in a session, accumulated history is modest. Synthesizing these: system prompt ~1,000 + history ~700 + current message ~300 ≈ 2,000 tokens total context for a typical production consumer chat request. This is consistent with the Epoch AI framing of a 'standard consumer chat query' as a short typed input plus modest session state, and with the LMSYS lower bound. Confidence is medium because no study directly measures total context window fill (system prompt + history) for ChatGPT.com / Claude.ai / Gemini app consumer traffic specifically — all available studies either measure raw user message length only (WildChat, LMSYS) or aggregate developer API traffic skewed by programming/agentic use (OpenRouter).

a.weighted_calculation: 0.60 * 3600 + 0.12 * 5700 + 0.22 * 3450 + 0.06 * 3950 = 2160 + 684 + 759 + 237 = 3840; rounded to 4200 to account for upward skew from memory injection, grounding snippets, and longer-session requests that are underrepresented in turn-1 estimates but material in aggregate token consumption

math_steps.notes: ChatGPT consumer product generated ~$8B in 2025 (66% of OpenAI's ~$12B 2025 revenue per BusinessOfApps). Adding Gemini app and Claude.ai consumer fractions (~$1-2B combined) yields ~$10B for the consumer_chat category. OpenAI total ARR ~$24B in April 2026 (SaaStr); enterprise >40% of mix (Sacra/OpenAI); consumer subscriptions (Plus, Pro, free-tier ad-equivalent) ~$10-12B. Using $10B as conservative floor.

math_steps.step: blended input price for consumer_chat inference
math_steps.value: $1.00 per 1M tokens (blended internal inference cost equivalent)
math_steps.notes: OpenAI's inference costs were $8.4B in 2025 serving all traffic (Sacra). GPT-5.4 API list price is $2.50/M input (pricepertoken.com); GPT-5.4 Mini ~$0.75/M; free-tier nano ~$0.20/M. The vast majority of 900M WAU are free users routed to mini/nano models. Paying subscribers (~50M) get premium models. Weighted-average internal cost for consumer chat blends to ~$1/M input tokens. Consumer chat is ~50% of total inference load → ~$4-5B of $8.4B total inference cost attributed to consumer chat.

math_steps.calc: $4.5B inference cost / ($1.00 per 1M tokens) = 4.5T input tokens/year
math_steps.notes: Using $4.5B as midpoint of the $4-5B consumer-chat share of OpenAI's $8.4B 2025 inference cost (Sacra). OpenAI dominates category (~80% share), so gross category input tokens ~5.6T. Using OpenAI alone for the primary calculation to stay grounded in disclosed figures.

math_steps.calc: 2.5B prompts/day (ChatGPT, confirmed by multiple sources including OpenAI directly) × 365 days = 912.5B requests/year for ChatGPT alone. Adding Gemini app and Claude.ai consumer at ~20% of ChatGPT volume gives ~1.1T category-wide. Using 1.0T as round category total.
math_steps.notes: Sources: DemandSage ('Over 2 billion daily queries are processed on ChatGPT'), TechnologyChecker ('ChatGPT receives approximately 2.5 billion prompts per day'), FatJoe ('ChatGPT also handles an estimated 2.5 billion prompts per day'). Cross-check: 900M WAU × ~25.7 messages/user/week (NBER paper cited by GetPanto) = 23.1B messages/week = 3.3B/day, somewhat higher than 2.5B/day, suggesting the 2.5B figure may already be slightly stale or conservative. Using 2.5B/day (= 912.5B/year) as the more conservative and more-cited direct figure.

math_steps.calc: 4.5T input tokens / 1.0T requests = ~4,500 tokens per request
math_steps.notes: Cross-check via subscription revenue route: $10B consumer revenue / 1T requests = $0.01/request. At $1/M blended input cost, $0.01 buys 10,000 input tokens — but subscription pricing is a revenue figure not a cost figure; gross margin ~33% means cost per request is ~$0.0033, implying ~3,300 tokens at $1/M. That alternative route gives ~3,000-3,300 tokens. The inference-cost route gives ~4,500. Averaging the two approaches suggests a range of 3,000-5,000 tokens, with 4,500 as the central estimate. Structural composition check: system prompt (~800 tokens) + memory/personalization layer (~500 tokens) + average 3-turn history at ~500 tokens/turn (~1,500 tokens) + current user message (~200 tokens) = ~3,000 tokens baseline for turn 4. Many sessions are early-turn (turn 1-2), pulling the average down; heavier users and multi-turn sessions pull it up. The ~4,000-5,000 range is consistent with a population-weighted average that includes short single-turn queries (system+message ~1,000 tokens) from the large free-tier base and longer multi-turn conversations from paying subscribers.

b.sanity_check: The implied 4,500 tokens/request is plausible and internally consistent. Structural decomposition: system prompt (~800T) + personalization/memory (~400T) + average chat history across all turns in a session (~2,500T weighted for turn distribution) + current user message (~200T) + occasional web search snippets for free-tier search queries (~600T weighted) ≈ 4,500T. The number is well above a bare single-message call (~1,000T) and well below the context window ceiling (400K-1M tokens for current GPT-5.x models). The free-tier mass (880M of 900M WAU) skews toward shorter early-turn conversations on lighter models, but the paid subscribers generate disproportionate token volume per session. A blended population average of ~4,000-5,000 tokens is consistent with (a) developer forum reports of 3,000-4,000 tokens per API call for basic chatbots with system prompts, (b) OpenAI's own web search integration adding 8,000 token blocks per search call (diluted by the fraction of queries using search), and (c) the session-length data showing average 12.5 minutes per web session, implying multiple back-and-forth turns. Confidence is medium rather than high because OpenAI does not publicly disclose per-request token counts, the revenue/cost split between consumer and enterprise is estimated, and model routing (which determines actual cost per token) is not publicly specified.

studies_cited.study_name: State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study with OpenRouter (a16z / OpenRouter)
studies_cited.what_it_measured: Average prompt tokens per request across 100 trillion tokens of real API traffic on OpenRouter (Nov 2024–Nov 2025), finding the cross-category mean grew from ~1,500 to ~6,000 tokens, with coding workloads exceeding 20K tokens and pulling the average up substantially.

studies_cited.study_name: WildChat: 1M ChatGPT Interaction Logs in the Wild (Zhao et al., ICLR 2024)
studies_cited.what_it_measured: Token statistics from 1 million real user–ChatGPT conversations (GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4), finding average user prompt token count of 295.58 tokens per turn and mean of 2.52 turns per conversation.

studies_cited.study_name: LMSYS-Chat-1M: A Large-Scale Real-World LLM Conversation Dataset (Zheng et al., ICLR 2024)
studies_cited.what_it_measured: Token statistics from 1 million real chatbot arena conversations across 25 LLMs, finding average user prompt of 69.5 tokens and average 2.0 turns per conversation (Llama-2 tokenizer).

studies_cited.study_name: How People Use ChatGPT (Chatterji et al., OpenAI / NBER Working Paper)
studies_cited.what_it_measured: Analysis of ~1.1 million randomly sampled consumer ChatGPT conversations (May 2024–June 2025), characterizing usage by topic: ~77% of messages fall into Practical Guidance, Seeking Information, and Writing — lightweight conversational tasks; non-work messages exceed 70% of all consumer messages.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: The OpenRouter 100T-token study reports a cross-category average of ~6,000 prompt tokens (late 2025), but this is heavily weighted by coding/agentic workloads that average 20K+ tokens (per the study's own note that 'programming drives most of this complexity, often requiring inputs exceeding 20,000 tokens'). OpenRouter also has no direct consumer chat traffic — it is a developer API aggregator. The OpenAI 'How People Use ChatGPT' study confirms that consumer ChatGPT is dominated by lightweight tasks (practical guidance, information seeking, writing), not coding or agentic workflows, so the 6K average does not apply. The WildChat dataset (296 tokens avg per user turn, 2.52 turns) and LMSYS-Chat-1M (70 tokens avg per user turn, 2.0 turns) provide direct measurements of real consumer chat message lengths, though both predate 2025 system prompt inflation and modern memory layers. To compute total context loaded at inference for a typical mid-session consumer_chat request: user message ~200 tokens (splitting WildChat 296 and LMSYS 70, skewing toward WildChat as more realistic) + system prompt ~1,000 tokens (typical for ChatGPT/Claude.ai/Gemini app, conservative estimate for consumer apps) + prior conversation history at avg turn 2 (~2 prior exchanges × ~500 tokens each = ~1,000 tokens) + memory/personalization layer in modern consumer apps ~300 tokens = ~2,500 tokens. Adding modest growth in prompt complexity since 2023-2024 datasets, rounding to ~2,700 tokens as the median production context at a typical mid-session turn. This is well below the 6K cross-platform API average (which is pulled up by coding) and consistent with the OpenRouter early-2024 baseline of ~1,500 for simpler developer requests, adjusted upward for system prompt and history accumulation present in consumer apps but absent in raw API calls.

history.rationale: Claude Code docs: edit-file 50-150K, 10-file project 50K, 500-file monorepo 500K+. Weighted mix (Copilot inline ~3K, chat 15K, refactoring 75K, full-agent 300K) lands 80-120K.

a.weighted_calculation: Weights sum to 1.00. Inline Copilot (0.22 * 4,200) + Copilot Chat (0.13 * 28,300) + Cursor (0.20 * 28,300) + Claude Code (0.18 * 50,500) + Bolt (0.10 * 78,300) + Lovable (0.07 * 28,300) + Replit (0.06 * 25,300) + Devin (0.04 * 50,500) = 924 + 3,679 + 5,660 + 9,090 + 7,830 + 1,981 + 1,518 + 2,020 = 32,702 ≈ 33,000. Rounded to 35,000 to reflect that inline-autocomplete's low context (0.22 weight at 4.2K) significantly drags the average down, but the category brief specifies 'coding agents' as the primary frame — if inline completions are included in share weighting, the blended figure is ~33K; if the focus is on agent/chat interactions (excluding raw autocomplete), the unweighted agent average is ~45K. Reported value of 35,000 represents the full weighted blend including inline completions.

b.sanity_check: The $60K revenue-weighted figure is coherent. Claude Code, which alone commands ~$2.5B ARR (40% of category), runs deeply agentic sessions where mid-session API calls carry 80–150K tokens (system + loaded files + tool-call history). One source notes 'referencing five medium-sized files can consume upwards of 30,000 tokens' and that 'a 10-step agentic task with 2,000-token tool results per step adds 20,000 tokens.' Claude Code rate-limit guides confirm individual API calls in active sessions routinely hit 50K–200K tokens. Cursor's mix of inline (low) and agentic (high) averages to ~60K for its paying revenue base. Copilot inline is frequent but cheap per call and contributes only ~$300M of the category's $6.2B revenue. The $60K estimate sits squarely between 'pure chat' (~2–5K) and 'full-context large codebase load' (~200K), appropriately reflecting a production-traffic weighted average across the category's revenue mix. The 2.5x–3x premium over a consumer chat session reflects real file loading and tool-output accumulation that defines coding agents.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: The 'coding_agents' category is internally bimodal: (A) inline autocomplete (GitHub Copilot inline, Cursor Tab), where context is a small window of surrounding code — typically 1,000–3,000 tokens of file context plus system prompt, yielding ~2,000–4,000 tokens per request; and (B) agentic/chat sessions (Claude Code multi-file edits, Devin autonomous tasks, Cursor Agent mode, Replit Agent, Lovable/Bolt scaffolding), where loaded files + tool outputs + session history accumulate to 20K–200K tokens per model call. The OpenRouter 100T-token study directly measured programming-category prompts as 'routinely exceeding 20K input tokens' in production (mid-2025 data), and the smol.ai summary of the same study reports the average for coding workloads on Claude (which owns ~60% of coding traffic) is 'over 20K tokens.' The Claude Code vs. Cursor benchmark found 33K tokens for an efficient agent and 188K for a less-efficient one on an identical real task — bracketing the agent sub-segment. The SWE-Pruner paper provides a complementary view: across all turns of a multi-step agent task, read operations alone consume ~2.89M tokens total, implying individual mid-task context windows in the 30K–80K range (with compaction). For a weighted typical production request across the full product portfolio — blending the large volume of lightweight autocomplete calls (~3K tokens each) with the smaller volume but token-dominant agentic calls (30K–100K) — the mix yields an average context of roughly 25,000–30,000 tokens per request. This is consistent with the OpenRouter >20K floor for the programming category and the 33K lower bound from the efficient-agent benchmark. The $0.30/day GitHub Copilot chat example (10 questions × 10K context each) also anchors the chat sub-mode at ~10K, below full agentic sessions. Midpoint of ~28K is the best defensible estimate. Confidence is medium because: (1) the OpenRouter study reports a floor ('>20K') not a precise mean for this sub-category; (2) the 33K/188K benchmark covers one task type and two specific agents; (3) inline autocomplete volume vs. agentic volume split is not published; and (4) the category spans products with very different architectures (Lovable/Bolt full-stack scaffolding vs. Copilot inline).

a.weighted_calculation: 0.22*2050 + 0.13*25300 + 0.25*28300 + 0.20*43300 + 0.08*24300 + 0.05*20300 + 0.04*60500 + 0.03*30300 = 451 + 3289 + 7075 + 8660 + 1944 + 1015 + 2420 + 909 = 25763 ≈ 28000 (rounded up to account for session growth beyond first turn, as the question targets a typical mid-session production request rather than turn-1 only)

math_steps.value: $7.3B blended category ARR (Claude Code ~$3B, Cursor ~$2.5B, GitHub Copilot ~$1B, Lovable ~$0.4B, Replit ~$0.2B, Devin/Cognition ~$0.175B, Bolt ~$0.07B); API-priced subset (excluding Copilot flat-sub) = ~$6.3B

$3.21 per 1M tokens (revenue-weighted across API-priced subset: Claude Code at $4/M Sonnet-4.6/Opus-4.7 blended; Cursor at $2.5/M routing across Anthropic+OpenAI+proprietary Composer; Replit/Lovable/Bolt at $2.5/M mostly Sonnet-class)

math_steps.calc: $6.3B / ($3.21 / 1M) = 1.96T input tokens/year across API-priced coding agent products

1.96T tokens / 56B LLM API calls = 35K tokens/call; 56B calls derived from 2M active users × 250 workdays × ~112 LLM calls/user/day (consistent with 5-10 agentic sessions/day each requiring 10-20 LLM calls, corroborated by observed Claude Code /context breakdowns showing 51K-76K tokens at mid-session with 20K fixed overhead + 10-30K accumulated messages; revenue-weighted across tiers: Claude Code 40% rev at ~60K, Cursor agent 25% at ~30K, Copilot chat 8% at ~8K, Copilot autocomplete 8% at ~2.5K, Devin 2% at ~80K, Replit/Lovable/Bolt 9% at ~15K, yielding weighted average of ~36K rounded to 35K)

b.sanity_check: 35K tokens is plausible for a category blending heavy terminal agents (Claude Code mid-session: system ~3K + tools ~17K + memory ~3K + accumulated tool outputs + messages = 40-70K observed via /context command) with IDE chat agents (Cursor: system + open files + RAG retrieval + history = 20-40K) and vibe-coding builders (10-20K per generation call). The category skews high relative to consumer chat because (1) code files are token-dense, (2) tool-call outputs from file reads accumulate in context, and (3) multi-file editing requires loading multiple files simultaneously. GitHub's own shift to token-based billing confirms that agent/chat requests regularly exceed plan pricing caps, consistent with 10K-100K token contexts. The implied 112 LLM API calls per active user per workday is high but consistent with background multi-agent parallelism (Cursor Background Agents, Claude Code /fleet, 3-agent teams each burning their own budget) that became standard in 2026. Claude Code Pro users get ~44K tokens per 5-hour window allocation, implying a single heavy session consumes that entire budget across ~10-20 LLM calls at ~2K-5K tokens each early in session, growing to ~40-70K tokens per call late in session — a session average consistent with ~35K/call.

studies_cited.what_it_measured: Token consumption patterns across distinct SDLC stages in a multi-agent software engineering framework (ChatDev/GPT-5), measuring input vs. output token shares and stage-level distributions across 30 tasks.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: The raw data points span a wide range that must be reconciled by tool type and measurement unit. (1) OpenRouter reports programming queries 'routinely exceed 20K input tokens' and 'Claude owns ~60% of coding workloads with average prompts over 20K tokens' — this is a floor anchored to mid-2025. (2) Requesty's production gateway data (the most directly relevant source: real coding agent API calls, not benchmarks) shows average input tokens per call rising from ~50K (May 2025) to ~200K (April 2026) across tools like Claude Code, Roo Code, and Cline — tools that are fully agentic and session-heavy. (3) Vantage's turn-by-turn model shows that a mid-session call (turn ~30) carries 25K–35K tokens, while a late-session call (turn ~50) approaches 100K–200K. (4) The Bai et al. paper confirms that input tokens dominate agentic coding at a 153:1 input:output ratio, and that total task consumption is orders of magnitude above chat — but that study measures full multi-step trajectories, not a single API call. The 'typical_context_tokens' definition specifies what is loaded for a TYPICAL SINGLE production API call (what fills the KV cache). The category is a composite: GitHub Copilot inline autocomplete is very low context (~2K–5K per request) and represents high request volume but low KV cache pressure per call; Cursor Composer/agent mode, Claude Code, and Devin/Replit Agent are heavy agentic tools with 25K–200K per call. Weighting: Copilot inline autocomplete likely represents the majority of raw request count but a minority of KV-cache-hours (since agents generate many more calls). For a typical request in aggregate across the named tools (Copilot chat + inline, Cursor agent, Claude Code, Devin, Replit, Lovable, Bolt), a reasonable production-weighted midpoint is ~60K tokens per API call as of mid-2026. This is consistent with the Requesty trajectory (started at 50K in May 2025, now trending toward 200K — a mid-2025-to-mid-2026 weighted average of roughly 80K for heavy agent tools, blended down to ~60K when including lower-context Copilot inline and simple chat-mode requests). Variance is high: simple autocomplete calls may be 2K–5K; a late-stage full-context Devin or Claude Code call may be 150K–200K. The 60K estimate targets the production-weighted median across the full named product set.

history.rationale: Microsoft Copilot Enterprise 64-128K windows, RAG fills selectively 10-30K. Harvey/Hebbia per-doc 30-100K. NOT the 1M max — production patterns rarely fill due to cost/latency/lost-in-middle.

b.sanity_check: 25,000 tokens (~18,750 words) is consistent with: system prompt (~2K) + RAG retrieval of 8–12 enterprise document chunks at ~1.5K each (~12–18K) + conversation history from prior turns (~3–4K) + user query (~200) = ~17K–24K total. This aligns with Glean's disclosed 32K/query anchor for a search-heavy platform, and sits below Harvey's document-review sessions (which can reach 50–100K when full contracts are loaded). The result also matches the production RAG practitioner benchmark of 5–20 chunks × 1.5–2K tokens each (7.5K–40K) plus overhead, with the central tendency around 15–30K. The economic math produces noisy estimates due to Copilot seat-based vs. token-based revenue mixing, but the Glean 20T-token disclosure provides a clean independent anchor. 25K is the best-fit central estimate for the mixed category.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: The OpenRouter/a16z study measures a developer API population that skews heavily toward programming (>50% of tokens by late 2025 are coding); enterprise_vertical_agents (Harvey legal, Hebbia finance, Glean knowledge, Sierra support, M365 Copilot Enterprise) are RAG-heavy but not primarily coding. Raw OpenRouter overall average (~6K tokens) is therefore too low for this category. However, the same study shows non-programming categories on OpenRouter remain 'relatively flat and low-volume', suggesting the coding uplift does not directly apply to enterprise knowledge-work agents. The correct anchor is the OpenRouter programming-category floor (~20K+) as an upper reference, adjusted downward for typical enterprise RAG access patterns. The enterprise RAG case-study data (post-pruning average of 25K tokens for a production technical documentation system; pre-pruning peaks of 100K+ for financial document queries) provides a direct production measurement. Structural decomposition for a typical enterprise vertical agent request: system prompt ~1–2K tokens + conversation history ~3–5K tokens (multi-turn enterprise sessions) + RAG-retrieved chunks (5–15 chunks × 1,000–2,000 tokens each = 10–30K tokens) + current user message ~200–500 tokens = roughly 15K–40K tokens per request. Enterprise verticals like Harvey (1–50 uploaded documents per thread) and Hebbia (full-document reasoning across contracts and filings) operate at the higher end of this range. Glean and Sierra (support-focused, more selective retrieval) skew lower. Critically, OpenRouter does NOT capture large enterprise deployments (Azure-hosted Copilot Enterprise, direct Anthropic 1P API contracts) per analyst critique, so the true enterprise figure is likely above the OpenRouter average but is validated by the production RAG case studies. A central estimate of ~35K tokens represents the weighted midpoint: selective retrieval (knowledge/support agents at ~15–20K) blended with document-heavy verticals (legal/finance agents at ~40–60K), with the production RAG benchmark at 25K after pruning as the most direct empirical anchor. Confidence is medium because no single study directly measures aggregate token fill for the exact enterprise_vertical_agents category as defined; figures are triangulated across the OpenRouter programming-category data, production RAG case studies, and structural decomposition.

The $25K estimate sits comfortably in the verified range and passes the bottom-up composition test.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: The OpenRouter 100T-token study reports an ALL-traffic average prompt length of ~6,000 tokens by late 2025 (grown ~4× from ~1,500 in early 2024). However, OpenRouter traffic is dominated by individual developer API calls and consumer-facing app traffic, including a large roleplay segment (~52% of OSS usage). The study separately reports that programming/agentic requests — the closest proxy for enterprise vertical agents — routinely exceed 20,000 input tokens, and that Claude coding workloads average over 20K tokens. Enterprise vertical agents (Harvey legal, Hebbia finance, Glean knowledge, Sierra support, Microsoft Copilot Enterprise, large RAG deployments) are structurally heavier than the OpenRouter average because every production request assembles: (1) a non-trivial system prompt with enterprise-specific instructions and tool definitions (typically 1,000–3,000 tokens, rising to 5,000+ when MCP tool definitions are included); (2) RAG-retrieved document chunks — production enterprise RAG typically retrieves 5–20 chunks of 500–2,000 tokens each, putting RAG context alone at 5,000–40,000 tokens; (3) conversation history from multi-turn sessions; and (4) the current user query. Non-coding enterprise verticals (legal document review, financial analysis, knowledge search, customer support escalations) sit between the 6,000-token all-traffic average and the 20,000+ token coding average. Legal and financial use cases (Harvey, Hebbia) regularly load full or partial contract/document text alongside RAG results, pushing individual requests toward 20,000–50,000 tokens. Support/knowledge agents (Sierra, Glean) are lighter but still include substantial RAG payloads (5,000–15,000 tokens). A production-weighted median across this category — accounting for document-heavy verticals at ~30–50K tokens and lighter support/knowledge agents at ~8–15K tokens — converges on approximately 25,000 tokens as the typical context fill. This aligns with the iternal.ai synthesis (5,000–15,000 for simple tool agents) being a floor, and the OpenRouter coding figure (20,000+) representing the reference point for document-intensive enterprise tasks. The 25,000-token estimate deliberately excludes the very long tail of Hebbia-style full-document-load scenarios (which can reach 100K+) that are not typical per-request but rather batch operations, and is anchored to the modal production request across the full enterprise vertical agent category.

history.rationale: OpenRouter empirical 6K skewed by short prompts. Production raw API typically 20-50K. Anthropic API B2B examples cite ~2K but integrations span 10-100K.

a.weighted_calculation: 0.40 × 5500 + 0.25 × 6100 + 0.10 × 1700 + 0.10 × 2750 + 0.08 × 2300 + 0.07 × 4500 = 2200 + 1525 + 170 + 275 + 184 + 315 = 4669 ≈ 4700, rounded to 4800 to account for upward skew from agentic workloads increasingly represented in the developer API mix (Anthropic engineering data shows agentic research tasks at 27K–44K tokens, pulling the tail up)

b.sanity_check: 7,500 input tokens corresponds to: system prompt (~1,000 tokens) + 3-turn chat history (~2,000 tokens) + moderate RAG or code snippet (~3,000 tokens) + current user message (~500 tokens) = ~6,500–7,500 tokens. This is consistent with a typical small-dev production app: a chatbot wrapper with a non-trivial system prompt, a few turns of retained history, and occasional retrieved context. It is NOT the bare single-turn call (which would be ~500–1,500 tokens) and NOT the heavy agentic Claude Code session (which would be 30,000–100,000 tokens). The OpenRouter empirical study found average prompts >6,000 tokens with coding Claude workloads averaging >20,000 tokens — our 7,500 sits between a light chatbot and a moderate dev tool, which matches the 'independent developer/small shop' description. The result is directionally confirmed by the economic math (~9,200 tokens) and the empirical floor (~4,000–6,000 tokens from OpenRouter), bracketing 7,500 as the central estimate.

c.category_adjustment_reasoning: OpenRouter is a pure developer API routing platform with 5M+ developers and no consumer UI wrapper — it is essentially the definition of the 'developer_raw_api' category, making its measured average of ~6,000 prompt tokens (as of Nov 2025, up 4x from ~1,500 in early 2024) the most directly applicable empirical anchor. No consumer-chat downward adjustment is needed. The platform's own category-level data shows programming workloads — now >50% of total token volume — routinely exceed 20K input tokens, while simpler developer API calls (single-turn text tasks, lightweight tool calls) anchor the lower end at ~1,500–2,500 tokens. The blended empirical average of ~6,000 already reflects this mix. An upward adjustment to ~8,000 tokens is applied for two reasons: (1) the trend line was still rising steeply through Nov 2025 and is ~6 months further along as of the as_of_date; (2) the 'developer_raw_api' category as defined here (independent developers, small shops doing direct API calls) skews more toward programming/agentic use cases than the full OpenRouter mix, which includes substantial roleplay traffic (52% of OSS usage) that tends to have shorter, flatter prompt sequences. The WildChat/CodeChat study (Zhong et al.) corroborates the short-prompt end (~296 median user tokens in raw developer turns before history accumulation), confirming that a long-tailed distribution — few very long coding sessions, many short calls — is what produces the ~6K mean. Confidence is medium rather than high because: (a) the programming-specific average (>20K) comes from a qualitative 'routinely exceed' characterization rather than a reported median; (b) OpenRouter may over-represent power users relative to the long tail of small indie developers; (c) the WildChat data predates the agentic-workflow inflection.
